committee: CC City Council Meeting of the Whole
overview: The Medford City Council Committee of the Whole serves as a deliberative body of all council members to conduct in-depth reviews of city finances, municipal ordinances, administrative appointments, and long-range planning initiatives. Over the span of 100 meetings running from November 2022 into October 2026, the committee conducted extensive annual budget hearings across all city departments, oversaw comprehensive zoning recodification efforts, advanced key environmental and licensing ordinances, and addressed litigation matters in executive session. It also regularly considered Community Development Block Grant and Community Preservation Act funding allocations and evaluated municipal staffing needs. Most recently, the committee advanced a procurement request for proposals for the next phase of citywide zoning updates and entered executive session to address pending municipal litigation.

threads.name: Annual municipal budget review
threads.summary: The committee conducts extensive hearings across municipal departments to review annual operating and capital budgets, beginning with the FY24 cycle that addressed financial software limitations, staff vacancies, and school district requests. For FY25 and FY26, the committee compiled collective priorities, scrutinized rising fixed costs such as employee health insurance and pensions, and addressed the fiscal fallout of expiring federal ARPA funds alongside structural deficits in the school budget. During the FY27 budget hearings, members engaged in detailed department-by-department evaluations spanning public safety, library pay equity, facilities maintenance, and enterprise funds, repeatedly referring recommendations and questions back to the administration for adjustments.

threads.name: Tree protection and Tree Committee ordinances
threads.summary: The committee initiated discussions on a multi-part tree ordinance in early 2023 to preserve the city canopy by regulating public shade trees, assessing private tree removals via zoning mitigation schedules, and creating a municipal Tree Committee. After referring drafts to departments, legal counsel, and community stakeholders for regulatory feedback and staffing cost estimates, the committee approved and reported out a separate Tree Committee ordinance in July 2025. In July 2026, the body amended the public tree ordinance regarding resident notifications and removal fines and referred it out to the regular meeting with outstanding questions for the DPW and legal counsel.

threads.name: Comprehensive zoning reform and planning updates
threads.summary: Following cleanup of the initial zoning recodification in late 2022, the committee shaped procurement and scopes for Phase Two comprehensive zoning, incorporating housing needs, digital mapping, and climate targets. The committee designated a selection group to retain Innes Associates in late 2023 and addressed specialized zoning overlays, including MBTA Communities compliance at Wellington Station. By late 2026, the committee considered an affordable housing linkage fee nexus study and authorized planning staff to advance a new consultant Request for Proposals for the next multi-year phase of citywide zoning updates.

threads.name: Outdoor dining regulation
threads.summary: Prompted by the expiration of state emergency orders, the committee drafted a permanent outdoor dining ordinance establishing clear standards for seasonal permits, ADA compliance, curb-level parklet construction, and animal policies. Subsequent sessions addressed severability clauses, tiered fee structures for sidewalks versus on-street parklets, alcohol alterations, and heater safety standards. In March 2023, the committee approved final amendments regarding liability insurance and fire code compliance and reported the ordinance out favorably to the full City Council.

threads.name: Food truck licensing reform
threads.summary: The committee took up a draft ordinance in early 2023 to replace the city's 2016 food truck policy with an administrative licensing process for stationary food trucks at one-day and special events. Legal counsel recommended bifurcating the framework so the Board of Health regulates sanitary standards while municipal ordinances govern public way usage and protect brick-and-mortar restaurants. In March 2024, the council retained the paper in committee to refine jurisdictional authority over public ways and municipal property.

threads.name: City charter revision
threads.summary: Beginning in spring 2023, the committee developed targeted amendments to the city charter to expand council authority to amend mayoral budget proposals, allow independent legislative staffing and legal counsel, and require confirmation of mayoral appointments. In 2024, governance charter work was incorporated into the council's governing agenda framework ahead of a comprehensive revision submitted by the mayor. In March 2025, the committee formally recommended a council composition consisting of five at-large seats and four district seats and referred the amended draft charter to the regular council meeting.

threads.name: Standard compensation and contracting standards
threads.summary: In early 2026, the committee considered an amendment to establish a standard compensation floor and benefits baseline for contracted city services, specifically targeting janitorial and security workers. The proposal was temporarily tabled and kept in committee to allow administration and procurement staff to evaluate wage data availability, labor peace terms, and legal enforceability. In April 2026, following debates over draft versions from legal counsel and council leadership, the committee reported an updated redlined ordinance to the regular meeting while requesting a written administration policy on legal advice procedures.

threads.name: Solid waste and composting services
threads.summary: The committee evaluated major shifts in the city's waste disposal contracts in early 2023, reviewing draft RFPs that proposed weekly curbside food composting paired with potential bi-weekly trash collection to control rising municipal costs. In mid-2023, DPW presented a proposed 10-year contract with Waste Management, along with fees for bulky items and preferred haulers for business districts, followed by amendments to the municipal solid waste ordinance. The new waste, recycling, and composting contracts were subsequently absorbed into the public works operating budget during FY25 and FY27 budget hearings.
